claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially has a high-temperature BCC structure.
Rapid cooling of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 induces transient, spinodal-like local compositional fluctuations.
The cooling-induced compositional fluctuations act as precursors for nucleation of secondary metastable phases during subsequent thermal exposure.
Slower cooling reduces the degree of departure from equilibrium relative to rapid cooling.
Slow cooling minimizes local compositional fluctuations in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Slow cooling primarily retains the high-temperature BCC structure.
Rapid cooling leaves excess free energy that does not dissipate uniformly.
Nonuniform dissipation of excess free energy causes short-range compositional clustering.
Short-range compositional fluctuations lower the nucleation barrier for secondary phases during later thermal exposure.
Microstructures produced by nonequilibrium rapid cooling can evolve substantially during subsequent high-temperature annealing.
Rapidly cooled samples will show an earlier onset of local compositional fluctuations than slowly cooled samples.
During identical isothermal holds, rapidly cooled samples will develop secondary phases earlier and at a higher volume fraction than slowly cooled samples.
The slow-cooled baseline will remain largely single-phase BCC with little or no secondary-phase nucleation during thermal exposure.
The proposed mechanism applies only when subsequent thermal exposure lies in a temperature window where metastable-phase nucleation is kinetically accessible.
The mechanism becomes inapplicable when cooling is slow enough to achieve full compositional homogenization.
Outside the metastable decomposition window, the driving force for local clustering is insufficient.
Cooling rate should be varied while all other processing conditions and the subsequent isothermal hold are controlled.
Failure of rapid cooling to increase compositional fluctuations or accelerate or increase secondary-phase nucleation relative to slow cooling would refute the hypothesis.
